items.title: Code-driven AI illustrations are more useful than images from dedicated image models
items.summary:
An interesting trend in frontier LLMs released in the second half of 2026 is that they tend to be much better at visual reasoning and creative "design" than their predecessors. If you ask these text-output models to create a 2D image (or a 3D model, as discussed here previously), you're very likely to get a useful result, and you may even get one that's aesthetically impressive. Most importantly, because these images are defined using code you (or the model) can make further edits to them without any of the weirdness that comes from iterating with a text-input, image-output model.

Poster design with Gemini 4 Neon

Gemini 4 Neon is getting some buzz for its 2D design skills, so I decided to try it out in AI Studio starting with the prompt:

Create an SVG poster promoting the Kakapo recovery project, research details first, make the poster look really cool and give it a 1970s graphic design

It took some iteration, partly because AI Studio doesn't render SVGs, so the models there can't spot visual mistakes without assistance.

Make the kakapo a bit more realistic, especially the face (image search for references)

Then:

[IMAGE] The text here doesn't fit the pill, fix it

And:

[IMAGE 2], [IMAGE 3] Also these

Here's the full transcript, exported from AI Studio as Markdown because I couldn't find a way to share a session that didn't require a Google login to view.

The end result is pretty solid:

AI Studio ran Google searches to find those numbers - I've checked and they are all correct. I like that it included red rimu tree fruit on the branch, since those are essential for the breeding season.

Whether or not you like the poster, the key thing about it is that everything is editable. You can directly edit the text in the SVG, or you can open it in Inkscape or Adobe Illustrator or Boxy SVG and edit it visually.

It's not just SVG

I have a well documented fondness for SVG generation, but it's not the only game in town.

A model hooked up to a coding agent environment can execute code to generate images. This opens up a whole realm of possibilities - generated image files, HTML and CSS, 2D HTML Canvas elements, Blender scripts, WebGPU shaders, PDF... any image mechanism that can be represented by a file on disk or the output of a script can be targeted by a model with a coding agent.

One of the reasons vibe game development has exploded recently is that models like Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Neon are capable of creating good-enough quality game assets - 3D models, textures, sprites, etc - entirely through writing code.

Building them with code means that tweaking, reusing, and remixing them is a case of the model writing even more code.

In comparison to image models

Most AI image generation tools use models that directly output bitmap graphics. Stable Diffusion, DALL-E, and Midjourney were early leaders in that space. The past ~15 months have seen the emergence of LLM-driven variants of this like Google's Nano Banana and OpenAI's ChatGPT Images. These have become competent at editing existing images and preserving details, which means you can iterate on a design over multiple conversation turns without it devolving into a mess.

They still have their limitations. They can produce weird glitches which become apparent when you zoom in on the details. They output text shapes directly from the model, which means you don't get the same guaranteed consistency that you would have with a real font-based typography system.

They are also inherently flat. You can describe changes you want in text, or draw annotations on an image to describe what you want, but you can't take control of an individual element or layer and directly manipulate it to get exactly what you want.

Update: There has been innovation here that I was unaware of when I wrote this article. Ideogram 4.0 for example claims "bounding-box layout control" through structured JSON prompting.

Images created through generated code solve all of those problems.

If you are generating photorealistic images then dedicated image models still have their place. For most of what I care about - explanatory diagrams, editable poster designs, UI components, visualizations, assets for games - code-driven images feel to me like a better bet.

I thought Anthropic was at a disadvantage

After Nano Banana and ChatGPT Images I thought Anthropic had a serious product gap on their hands.

OpenAI and Google both had excellent image generation models as part of their product suites. They even had generative video models - Google still does with Veo and now Omni, OpenAI sunset Sora.

The business world still runs on PowerPoint, so if you're selling an enterprise contract having a great image generation model seemed to me like it would be an expected feature for many customers.

These days Claude can quite happily churn out visually compelling presentations and website designs, and Claude Design provides a full design system platform. All built around code-driven images!

This feels like another variant of the bitter lesson: I was convinced a specialist image model was necessary to serve customers with design problems. It turns out the text-output LLMs just kept getting more capable until they could handle visual design by writing code.

items.title: AWS Challenger: Trainium3 Inference and Microarchitecture Deep Dive
items.summary: Better Perf TCO vs NVIDIA GB300, First Principles Physics-Based Architecture, High MFU and MBU, UBenchX, Low Latency, Alisa Liu vs Eileen Gu
items.story_key: story|title:aws challenger trainium3 inference and microarchitecture deep dive
items.content_excerpt: The Nvidia GPU was originally built to shade pixels, and every Nvidia generation since 2017 has bolted on another piece of AI-specific hardware to fix the bottleneck the previous one exposed. Volta added Tensor Cores, Hopper added TMA for tile data movement between HBM and SRAM, and Blackwell added Tensor Memory for accumulating. Nvidia removed many hardware units that are required to render graphics for their datacenter GPUs In comparison, the Trainium microarchitecture is built ground-up specifically for ML workloads, with tiles as a first-class primitive instead of having a sea of threads and then bolting on tensor/tile compute and data movement engines. Trainium3 behaves the way the physics says it should. In this past this meant software was a humongous challenge, but now no longer. 7 months later, Trainium 3 and TPUs are live on InferenceX , both trading blows or even winning vs Nvidia GB300 in cost to generate tokens at TCO. We will dive into those details below. This advantage is not purely due to Amazon’s ultra low cost supply chain. It's also due to microarchitectural decisions, which we will dive into in this post. For example, using the Trainium Descriptor Generation Engines (DGE), the equivalent of Nvidia TMA and AMD MI455X TDM, our microbenchmarks show that Trainium can reach peak HBM bandwidth utilization (MBU) at small message sizes, which is not possible on Nvidia GPUs. Furthermore, our testing covers cycle-level SRAM scratchpad latency and bandwidth testing (SBUF to PSUM), rack-scale bandwidth and latency microbenchmarks, attention exponential testing, and the precise cycle-level latency of different shapes, including how different attention head_dim (K) would affect the percentage of roofline. Every result comes from UBenchX, our microbenchmark suite, and we model each unit from first principles before we measure it. We thank Nafea Bshara (Co-Founder of AWS Annapurna Labs), Ron Diamant (Trainium Chief Architect), Michael Shteinbok, Armin Ebrahim and the rest of their team for helping teach us their architecture and validate our benchmark experiments. Star the InferenceX & UBenchX GitHub repository if you find the open-source benchmark and data useful ! InferenceX is the only inference benchmark in the world to have TPUv7, OpenAI Jalapeño, Nvidia Rubin NVL72, AMD, and now, Trainium3. AgentX measures Trainium3 on a production end-to-end agentic inference workload. This is achieved by replaying real coding-agent sessions against a Trainium3

items.title: 1. Don't make decisions based on benchmarks.  They have too many flaws.
items.summary:
1. Don't make decisions based on benchmarks.  They have too many flaws. 

2. Use your own evals 

3. If you must use benchmarks, look at the data.  Looking at just one failed task is often enough to uncover major issues.  TBH, you'll be convinced not to trust benchmarks if you do

Quoting @HamelHusain: Looking at the decision index benchmarks and wow pervasive overfitting of models!!! 

I'm more likely to use a model that has a high & consistent public + private score vs. those with a huge drift

Also, beware - the models are sorted by public scores in the individual benchmark (https://x.com/HamelHusain/status/2125701624320680214)

items.title: Swarms, Flocks, Gangs: How to build, train, and evaluate multi-agent systems
items.story_key: story|title:swarms flocks gangs how to build train and evaluate multi agent systems
items.content_excerpt: This is an aspirational blog series for aspirational readers. We (us, the community, you) want to build our own agent swarms because they're exciting, challenging, and increasingly capable. Furthermore, it would be extremely cool if we could train our own agents to work in a swarm. And exponentially cool if those swarms used small and affordable models. That's what we'll do in this series! Each blog post will include some context on building swarms, alongside reproducible examples that you can run on Hugging Face Jobs. This post's example takes about five hours on two H200s, which costs roughly $50. Multi-Agent Systems are hard to get working. Adding agents changes the agent's context, the budget, and in turn the complexity of the whole system. Mixing agents' context together through communication is not an inherent performance boost compared to a single agent. The model needs to learn to communicate through training. How do we define what models should learn? And which model weights do we update when we're dealing with many agents? In this series, we'll work through those problems with an educational overview and practical examples. Each post will introduce a question, build a small system, and examine what happens and how you can reproduce it. This first example starts with four agents, a shared language model, and a simple verifiable task. It's ideal to implement yourself, to tinker with, and to learn from. We've heard a lot about swarms over the past few months, both good and bad. In September this year, OpenAI announced that a swarm of roughly 10,000 agents had found a singularity in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations, one of the Millennium Prize problems. A smaller group of nearly 100 agents had already disproved regularity for the unforced 3D Euler equations, a closely related open problem. But swarms don't always work on the problems we want them to. METR's investigation of the Hugging Face incident found that around 1,200 OpenAI agents, which were supposed to be isolated, had found a way to exchange over 70,000 messages and files. Around 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face while looking for ways to fool their benchmark's scorer, without instruction to do so. A big swarm isn't, by itself, evidence that cooperation helped. Noam Brown estimates that less than 10% of the Navier-Stokes result came from multi-agent cooperation. items.title: Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference
items.story_key: model:nemotron|ver:3.5|title:building on nemotron 3 5 parse open data fine tuning and faster inference
items.content_excerpt: We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse , a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents. Now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference . We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion. Parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content. Tables and charts become structured records that can power downstream document processing applications. Figure 1. Actual model output from a synthetic operations brief, showing the connection between the page and its structured representation. This latest version of Parse significantly extends its ability to read charts and tables, especially in more difficult and ambiguous cases. For example, bar charts or other plots that do not have any marked numeric values. The model is able to infer values by looking at the axes and height of the bar to derive these. Tables can be especially tricky because the structure is so meaningful, a shifted row or column can totally change the interpretation and meaning. These advancements have been largely powered by synthetic data generation, rendering variations of charts and tables with known ground truth and then training our model to reverse this process. Synthetic Charts V1 — 9.98M examples : rendered charts and structured annotations for learning categories, series, and numerical values. Synthetic Tables V1 — 1M examples : rendered HTML tables with targets that preserve rows, columns, headers, and cell relationships. OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 — 7.9M examples : synthetic document pages with Parse-format targets across varied fonts and layouts, for multilingual OCR and structured page reading. Each release includes images, annotations, generation documentation, and the training format. Use these pairs to fine-tune document models or create new variations for a target document type or language. We trained Parse 3.5 with two phases of training. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) spanning text, layout, tables, charts, and multilingual documents. Learning to predict structured targets established the general capability of reading

items.title: RoboEvo$^2$: Recursive Robot Self-Improvement via Harness-Policy Co-Evolution
items.summary: Robots should adapt to unfamiliar environments and acquire new skills through interaction, then execute those skills efficiently with practice. Vision-language-action policies provide efficient control, but often need additional human demonstrations to handle unfamiliar settings; reasoning agents can discover solutions using broad prior knowledge and robot-control APIs, but repeated deliberation and repair are costly. Inspired by human learning through reasoning and practice, we propose RoboEvo$^2$, a framework for recursive harness-policy co-evolution. In Policy-to-Harness (P2H) evolution, policy failures guide a coding agent to search complementary Code, Code+ICL, and Code+Policy routes, consolidating verified solutions into reusable skills, routing strategies, and experience memory. In Harness-to-Policy (H2P) evolution, verified trajectories provide supervised training, while Counterfactual Preference Distillation (CPD) teaches the policy to favor successful corrections over failures from the same starting state. The improved policy provides stronger motor skills for subsequent search, while its remaining failures redirect harness evolution, closing the reciprocal loop. Through recursive co-evolution without additional human demonstrations, RoboEvo$^2$ improves standalone success from 11.0% to 84.1% and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5% on LIBERO-PRO, with similar gains and reduced agentic costs on RoboTwin C2R. Further experiments demonstrate autonomous task acquisition, cross-embodiment harness transfer, and 95.0% hybrid success on the Unitree G1-D. Our models and code will be publicly released.

items.title: Why I'm Bullish on MCP for 2027
items.summary: Early MCP deserved its backlash. Code Mode, typed outputSchema, native multimodality, Agent Skills inside MCP, always-on MCP Events, and MCP Apps are turning it into the integration layer for agent harnesses in 2027.
items.story_key: story|title:why i m bullish on mcp for 2027
items.content_excerpt: MCP went through the full hype cycle in the last 18 months. Early excitement turned into backlash and confusion fast, with context bloat as the main complaint. When Skills arrived, most developers moved to CLIs and progressive disclosure instead. I never believed in that, and that sentiment is now changing. At Linear and Notion , agents now create roughly half of all issues (~2.4M/week) and pages, with Notion reporting 60x MCP traffic growth. At Atlassian , MCP handles over 5M tool calls per workday, and 44% of those users sit outside software teams where CLIs were never an option. At Neon , agent usage over MCP grows 14% week over week, and even Apple now ships local MCP servers for Pages, Numbers, and Keynote. The protocol is healthy and actively improving. The 2026-07-28 spec dropped stateful sessions and added official extensions, and clients are getting smarter about how they use them. Real tasks almost always take more than 1 tool call, e.g. you list open issues, grab details, check errors, and write a summary. With plain tool calling, every step needs another model turn and dumps information into the context. Joining data across 2 MCP servers uses the model's context as memory for intermediate payloads. Code Mode is changing how agents call MCP servers. Instead of putting 50 tool schemas into the prompt and calling 1 tool per turn, the harness gives the model a sandbox and exposes MCP tools as callable functions. It's already becoming the default in OpenCode 2.0, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Pi, and Factory Droid. Code Mode works best when the model knows what a tool returns before writing code. When an MCP server declares outputSchema alongside inputSchema , the client can generate typed stubs upfront and pass back structuredContent directly. The model chains multiple calls in 1 script, filters and joins in memory where compute is cheap, and returns only what matters. Compared to CLIs, MCP servers are natively multimodal. A tool call can return typed structuredContent for code alongside separate image, audio, or embedded resource blocks. Auth is also cleaner. CLIs and raw curl force you to store API keys on disk or in environment variables with broad permissions. An MCP client handles per-user OAuth 2.1 login flows and scoped tool permissions outside the sandbox, so connecting a remote SaaS product works without handing raw credentials to the agent. items.title: vLLM Day-0 Support for ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview: Plugin Deployment and E2E Inference Acceleration
items.summary: vLLM supports Baidu's ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview on day 0 through the vLLM-ERNIE plugin on the released vllm==0.32.0 wheel, with structure-aware kernel fusion, FlashIndexer, W4A8 QAT and DSpark speculative decoding.
items.story_key: model:vllm|ver:5.5|variant:flash,preview|title:vllm day 0 support for ernie 5 5 flash preview plugin deployment and e2e inferen
items.content_excerpt: The Baidu ERNIE team has worked with vLLM to bring day-0 support for ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview to vLLM. ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview is a sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 280B total parameters and 14B activated per token. It supports a 1M-token context, thinks before it answers, and uses tool calling to carry out long-horizon Agent tasks. vLLM supports the model on release day through the vLLM-ERNIE plugin, a standalone package that you install into the same environment as the official vllm==0.32.0 wheel. Install the released vLLM wheel and the plugin into the same environment. vLLM discovers the plugin automatically through its vllm.general_plugins entrypoint, so there is nothing to import or configure. The following command serves the default FP4 weights on a single 4-GPU node, with DSpark speculative decoding drafting 7 tokens per step: To turn off thinking for a request, pass "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} . Launch commands for 1M context, attention TP and PD disaggregation are in the vLLM-ERNIE README and the vLLM recipe . ERNIE 5.5 Flash was designed with inference cost as a primary goal from the start, weighing activated compute, KV cache size and long-context overhead together. Every component, from the attention structure and residual connections to the MoE layers and the output head, was redesigned around that goal. For design and training details, see the ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview blog . ERNIE 5.5 Flash introduces several new structures in attention and MoE: low-rank cross-head post-mixing (VHA post-mix), Multi-Router Latent MoE, the MultiMax output head and sigmoid output gating. When implemented op by op from their mathematical definitions, these structures produce many intermediate tensors and pay for them in memory traffic and kernel launches. For each structure, we designed a dedicated fused kernel around its compute and memory-access profile, and folded everything that can be precomputed into the weights at load time. The fused kernels run 1.55× to 6.53× faster than naive implementations. Together, these fusions cover the full forward pass of ERNIE 5.5 Flash, from attention and MoE routing to the output head. They cut the number of kernel launches and the round trips of intermediate tensors through GPU memory while keeping the numerics aligned, and they underpin the model's high inference performance. The Baidu ERNIE inference team developed FlashIndexer, a lightweight indexer acceleration built on dynamic head routing

items.title: Hierarchical Graph Metanetworks
items.summary: The emerging field of weight space learning has demonstrated the potential to enable metanetworks, i.e. models that process neural network (NN) data, to support several steps of the machine learning lifecycle, from model optimisation to evaluation and adaptation. However, this potential has yet to materialise beyond small-scale MLPs or CNNs: most current models, including message-passing based graph metanetworks (GMNs), operate exclusively at the finest level of granularity, processing every neuron and weight of the input model. Their cost therefore scales with the number of parameters. Yet NNs are inherently organised hierarchically, with neurons forming layers and layers forming blocks and modules. Additionally, several of their properties, such as Lipschitz upper bounds and generalisation measures, are compositions of layer- and block-level quantities. To incorporate this inductive bias, we introduce Hierarchical Graph Metanetworks (H-GMNs), which leverage the input architecture's hierarchy to coarsen and refine the graph using permutation-symmetry-preserving pooling and un-pooling layers. Further, we extend H-GMNs to Transformers by introducing a graph construction that preserves permutation symmetries and enables multi-level pooling. Our evaluation includes new ResNet-18, ViT and varying ViT model zoos of up to 86M parameters, on tasks spanning model evaluation (an analytic Lipschitz bound proxy, generalisation and robustness prediction), testing (backdoor detection) and editing (pruning). Experimental results show that, compared to non-equivariant alternatives and flat GMNs, H-GMNs are markedly more sample-efficient, and their cost remains nearly constant as metanetwork depth grows, allowing deeper and more expressive processing where flat GMNs run out of memory, without compromising accuracy, which in certain cases considerably improves.

items.title: Make the Adversary Spend More: Stateful Deception as a Cost-Exchange Primitive for AI-Era Cyber Defense
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are transforming the economics of intrusion by reducing the attacker's cost to scan and adapt, while tempting defenders into unbounded compute. We argue that cyber deception should be judged by the cost exchange it imposes, not by realism or detection, and that the primitive making that exchange favorable is adversary-specific persistent state. Rather than a honeypot that resets or merges sessions, each recognized adversary re-enters the world it believes it has compromised, kept coherent with its own past actions and isolated from every other adversary, while the language model acts only as a constrained renderer of explicit state, never as its store. We formalize the trade-off as a Deception Exchange Rate (DER), relating mission-weighted adversary effort burned to defender resources spent, and instantiate it in an SSH honeypot pairing Cowrie with a local LLM. In this paper, we focus on the defender-side evaluation of that exchange, while specifying, but not yet measuring, per-adversary state and the adversary side of the DER. Across five open-weight models, deterministic-layer and prompt optimizations cut per-session defender cost by around 63% against a naive all-LLM decoy.

items.title: Introducing Search for Agents
items.summary: Flip one toggle to make your site searchable by AI agents — complete with automatic content indexing, a discoverable search API, and native HTTP QUERY support.
items.content_excerpt: AI Search , our service that indexes your content and lets you add search to any application or agent without having to build an entire retrieval infrastructure, has supported adding your website as a data source for a while now, automatically crawling, converting and indexing its pages. Still, setting up an AI Search instance for your website requires manually creating and configuring it initially, and then doing all the integration work to get the search endpoints available from your domain and to make sure that agents know where to find the index and know how to use it. Today we're introducing Search for Agents , which puts that setup behind a toggle in your Cloudflare dashboard. Turn it on for your zone, and our service will create your AI Search instance, start indexing your content, and make search discoverable and available from your own domain. The idea follows naturally from Markdown for Agents , where Cloudflare's network converts any HTML page to Markdown in real time for enabled zones using content negotiation headers. Similarly, Search for Agents leverages the power of AI Search by automatically creating an index for your zone and exposing APIs that any AI agent can discover and use to search your website, under your domain, all done at the network level. You can enable Search for Agents using the API, or by going to the dashboard in your zone page, under Quick Actions : Search for Agents is available to all customers, including Free (with limits ). Once it’s enabled, Cloudflare will automatically create an AI Search instance, start crawling and indexing the content in your zone. Refer to our developer documentation to understand how the crawling process works. You can access your instance directly from this page, or by going to directly to your account’s AI > AI Search instances view: The AI Search instance for your zone is created with default settings, but you can enable reranking or change configuration options like cache settings at any time. Refer to our documentation for the full list of options. Once AI Search indexes your content, you or any agent on the Internet can start using Search for Agents, subject to your domain settings (e.g. your bot management settings, AI Crawl Control and web application firewall ( WAF ) configurations). Search isn't much use if the agents don’t know it's there. To facilitate discoverability, Search for Agents automatically advertises the search endpoint on every page of your site.
